dropout consumer wired (appendLostSamples in src/data/gaps.ts). It was dead for two rounds and the cause was structural, not a bad guard: with no samples appended the lost span has zero width in store coordinates, so there was nothing for noteGap to mark. Decision taken - append filler for the lost samples so the store's axis keeps tracking device time. The filler repeats the LAST KNOWN SAMPLE rather than zeroing; zeros invent a rising edge at the gap's end, which sits outside the gap where edges() reports it as real (MEASURED: exactly 16 spurious edges, 1 per channel). Pinned end to end in offline-test.ts: 383948 delivered + 50 lost = store length 383998, one gap at [255948, 255998). Mutation-checked both ways - zeroed filler turns the edge check red, skipping the append throws 'gap [255948,255998) outside 0 <= start < end <= 255948', which is the zero-width problem stating itself. Lost-sample count now shows in the capture panel while recording. Hardware has still never produced a short transfer, so this runs only against the scripted device

USB transport moved into a Dedicated Worker (318fe2f), which is the libsigrok shape - URBs reaped on a thread that has nothing else to do, so a 20-38 ms page stall cannot starve a 19.6 ms queue at 32ch/200M. The worker transfers each chunk's buffer and does not refill that URB slot until the page acks, so the existing lagChunks bound still holds; requestDevice stays a page gesture and the worker finds the grant via getDevices(), falling back to the in-page transport with the reason recorded when it cannot. One bundling trap found and contained: './usbWorker.ts?worker&inline' is a Vite-only specifier and importing it from workerTransport.ts broke the offline suite's esbuild bundle (exit 1, no test output) - it now lives only in usbWorkerSpawn.ts, installed through installUsbWorkerSpawn(), so device/ is esbuild-bundlable again. Verified with no board: 139 offline checks (18 new), tsc/vite/dist/single-file portable smoke all clean, and in the real browser the worker spawned and answered in 11 ms with 'the 359f:3032 device is not visible to this worker'. BLOCKER: the 32U3 is off the bus and needs a physical replug before any of this can be measured against libsigrok at 100M/200M

Worker transport made honest and measurable (d99929b, dff4219, 8c1568e). The window the split buys, now arithmetic instead of a claim: each transfer is 7.82 ms of device time at 32ch/100M and 3.91 ms at 200M, so depth 5 covers 19.6 ms on the page - the completion callback IS the re-arm and a blocked page cannot run it - while the worker keeps reaping until completed+inFlight hits lagChunks=20, which is 78.2 ms at 200M / 156.5 ms at 100M for 62.6 MB. 4x the old window against the 38.1 ms worst stall measured here. Diagnostics fixed to match: threadLabel is passed as 'worker' by the page transport and is sticky (bench restarts the loop without options), so an abort can no longer call the worker's thread 'the page thread'; the page runs its own LoopStallWatch for every capture (pageStallMaxMs/pageStalls) and appends its line to a bench reply, because the worker's reply can only describe the worker. 143 offline checks. Re-read protocol.c (8.21): training probe, timeout_count_limit = num_transfers_used, re-arm pushed to an unbounded GAsyncQueue before the consumer sees it - all confirmed against this transport. The one mechanism with no WebUSB equivalent is libusb's per-transfer timeout (protocol.c:405, ~36 ms at 200M) that turns a half-dead pipe into slow transfers the abort rule catches; WebUSB transferIn has no timeout, so a transfer the device never fills stays pending until release. That is a fidelity gap, not a tuning one, and the first suspect if hardware shows transfers stopping with no error. 32U3 still absent from the bus (only 359f:4201 thermal camera and a Sipeed CMSIS-DAP probe are attached); one physical replug unblocks the 100M/200M comparison

The 32ch/200M claim is now measured, not argued (02f2a1f, NOTES 8.22). Built a board-free A/B: ClockStreamDevice samples on its OWN clock with a FIFO, which the offline suite's scripted device cannot do - there, transferIn completes when the host asks, so a host that stops reading is never punished - and tools/windowHarness.ts runs both transports against it with the shipping driver, the shipping createSampleStore and the capture panel's sink, injecting a page stall that stands in for the 38 ms append+GC. Result at 2 s of 32ch/200M with a 40 ms stall every 300 ms: page transport aborts 97 ms in at 546 MB/s (its own message: 'the page thread was blocked, worst 46.8 ms, the queue covers 19.6 ms'); worker transport delivers all 517 transfers at 100.0% of 800 MB/s, 0 short, 0 slow, 0 lost, while the page was blocked 38.4 ms. Sweep of the worker arm finds the edge at 80 ms (clean at 60, losing data at 80 and 100, aborts at 120) - the same number 8.20 derived from lagChunks x transfer arithmetic, now measured by a device counting the milliseconds it had nothing to fill. The harness caught two of its own errors on the way, both recorded: it first used PlanarSampleStore instead of createSampleStore (32 channels are interleaved in the app; planar costs 8.5 ms against a 3.9 ms budget) and the scripted device first generated 3.13 MB through a 25 MB boxed number array (165 ms per chunk). Also re-confirmed 100M as the control: both arms complete at 399.4 MB/s. 143 offline checks, tsc/build green. 32U3 still off the bus; the hardware comparison still needs a physical replug

The tool that measured the 32ch/200M question was the thing breaking the board (9f8df1d, 017adbd, NOTES 8.23). The 32U3 came back on the bus today (Bus 002 Device 108, 359f:3032, S/N 202608052052) and the first hardware number was a good one: `bench 2 32 100` through the worker, on the page's own device grant, held 398.0 MB/s of 400 - 255 transfers, 0 short, 0 slow, longest idle gap 0.00 ms, page thread never blocked - which answers 8.19's open question (a Dedicated Worker does see a page-granted device) on real hardware. Then `bench 2 32 200` failed three times in a row and a 0.3 s/100M run afterwards delivered 0 bytes: the board was wedged. Cause found in the bench itself, and it is exactly the failure NOTES 8.6 describes: bench waited out its duration and then called stop() on a device that was STILL PRODUCING, so the host cut a live producer off, the FIFO overran, and the bulk endpoint went silent until a replug. A measuring tool must not be the thing that breaks the device. Two consequences: (1) the three 200M failures are not evidence about 200M - the board had already been through a 100M bench that ended by cutting it off, so 200M has to be taken FIRST on a freshly replugged board; (2) the 200M failure was reported as 'the worker answered with no console result', because the worker's {kind:'failed'} message was being replaced by a sentence about the reply's shape - both usbControl and getStats now re-throw the worker's own sentence (that one is verified on the wedged board in the page: 'delivered no data within 578 ms of RUN ... unplug it'). Fixes: bench arms R32_SAMPLE_LEN with the requested sample count and waits seconds+400 ms before stop, so the device ends the run itself; and stop() now recognises a device that already delivered everything its verified limit allowed and releases the interface immediately instead of waiting out STOP_TIMEOUT_MS for tail reads that are NAKs - that is 1.5 s and a release/re-claim pair saved on every timed capture the device finished, safe because the armed total is the device's own count and can only be matched after the last data-carrying transfer has been consumed. The scripted clock device had to learn to reject its post-limit reads on release the way libusb reports a cancelled URB; handing the driver a promise that never settles is what hung the first version of that check. 147 offline checks (4 new, none lost), tsc/vite build green. The board is wedged right now and answers every control transfer with R32_FLAG=0x00 and nothing on the bulk endpoint; clear-fifo and a CTRL=0 write do not revive it, so it needs a physical replug before the 200M-first measurement (script ready: /tmp/lwcdp/_hw.js)

The fixed 32ch@200M measurement, and the tool that has to answer the rest (cb20938, 738a2f3, 82f1a9a, 680b89a, ed5f146, NOTES 8.24). On a freshly replugged board (device 109) the simplest possible configuration - `bench 1 32 200`, worker transport, no sink, pure pipe - gives steady 532.5 MB/s of 800 with read p50 6.00 ms against the device's own 3.91 ms, 0 short reads, rearm p50 0.10 ms, maxIdleGap 0 and 0 thread stalls: nothing on this side is waiting, the time is inside Chromium's USB path between the device filling a read and this transport being handed it. The control is libsigrok on the same board, port and machine: nat.200m-8000ms delivered exactly 6,400,000,012 bytes in 8 s (800 MB/s, 2046 transfers, 0 transfer timeouts) and 32ch@100M delivered 1,200,000,012 bytes in 3 s, so the device, the link and the port are not the difference. The browser does reach 32ch@100M (398.0 of 400 MB/s measured in the worker) and does not reach 32ch@200M. Every browser attempt at 200M still ends with the board wedged - including with the device-side length limit armed and the fixed bench - because the device offers 800 while the host drains ~530, so the backlog outruns the FIFO before any abort rule can fire; recovery is a physical replug, and `bench 0.5 16 50` (100 MB/s) then delivers nothing. Software recovery was tried on this wedge state and does not exist: CTRL.RST (which the shipping driver never writes) leaves FLAG=0x00 and the pipe silent, clear-fifo has nothing latched to clear, and 4ch@10M delivers 0 bytes. The open question 8.7 left is now the only one that matters - is that ~500 MB/s a per-read cost (a turnaround a different read size or depth amortises) or a per-byte cost in Chromium's copy chain (in which case no geometry reaches 800 and 32ch/200M is out of reach for WebUSB on this host)? The instrument is now in the repository: `bench` takes [depth] [transferBytes] and reports the geometry it measured, its seconds floor is 5 ms (20 ms at 32ch/200M is 16 MB, inside the 15.6 MiB of reads already in flight), and `npm run bench:geometry` sweeps libsigrok's own probe geometry plus the largest reads that fit the 16 MiB usbfs budget plus four size/depth trades, each as repeated slices capped at 80% of the queued-read budget so a run that measures a host slower than the device cannot overrun the FIFO and cannot cost a replug. The 100M geometry is the method control. 151 offline checks green (4 new), tsc/build green. Also worth recording: only Chromium implements WebUSB on this machine (Firefox 155 has no WebUSB), so the product's ceiling is Chromium's USB path, not a choice of browser. Blocked on one physical replug to run the sweep.

Chromium's own source answers the *shape* of the 32ch/200M question, and the sweep now carries the one geometry that could still pay (NOTES 8.25). A `transferIn` above 64 KiB is copied twice by construction: the device service allocates a fresh RefCountedBytes per call, feeds the reply as a mojo_base::BigBuffer, and BigBuffer's span constructor 'Always copies the contents of |data| into some internal storage' - and above kMaxInlineBytes = 64 KiB that storage is a fresh shared memory region whose pages the kernel zeroes on first touch; the renderer then does DOMArrayBuffer::Create(data), the second full copy. That is a per-BYTE tax, and 8.24's numbers fit it exactly: 6.00 ms observed minus the device's 3.91 ms is 2.09 ms for 3,129,344 B = 0.68 us/KiB, and a per-byte tax at that rate gives 1/(1/800MBps + 0.68us/KiB) = 521 MB/s at *any* read size, against 532.5 MB/s measured. A per-READ tax would have shown a curve climbing toward 800 instead. So `npm run bench:geometry` gained four rows that bracket the threshold at equal queue size - 32 x 131072 (just over) against 64 x 65536 (inline, same 4 MiB), plus 120 x 65536 and 200 x 65536 - because 64 KiB and below never leaves the mojo message and is the only read size the two hypotheses disagree about; every earlier row was 782,336 B and above. Same source, second bound: kWebUSBTransferSizeLimit (on by default) refuses any single transfer over 32 MiB, so 'one enormous read' tops out at 32 MiB even with usbfs_memory_mb raised - still ~520 MB/s at that per-byte rate. If the 64 KiB rows come back at ~530 the answer for the product is 32ch/100M over WebUSB plus a native backend for 200M (the user's own AppImage is already that backend); if they jump, the transport switches to <=64 KiB reads with a deep queue and the per-chunk cost in the app (12,500 chunks/s into the store) becomes the next thing to fix by batching. 151 offline checks, tsc and vite build green. Still blocked on one physical replug: device 109 is in 8.8's W1 state (0 bytes at every rate), and CTRL.RST, clear-fifo, clearHalt on EP 0x82, USBDevice.reset() and a raw USBDEVFS_RESET on the usbfs node were all tried again on it this session without bringing the pipe back.

The browser's ceiling was never the line rate: it is 1 MiB, and WebUSB on this host DOES receive 32ch/200M continuously once the reads are under it (e141170, NOTES 8.26). The instrument was the wedge itself - the board's sampler is dead (W1) but `aux 5 = 1` (RB_TEST_UPLOAD, the vendor's USB-max-speed mode) still pushes bytes through EP 0x82, so `bench` now takes a sixth word for the source and `bench 0.5 32 200 200 65536 usbmax` measures the HOST with a free-running producer. Swept with the queue held at 12 MiB: 64 KiB x 200 = 927 MB/s, 128 KiB = 967, 256 KiB = 927, 512 KiB = 909, 768 KiB x 16 = **1,599,602,688 B in 1649 ms = 970 MB/s over two seconds** (2034 calls, 0 short, 0 slow, 0 idle gap), 956 KiB = 921 - and then 1 MiB = 477-533 MB/s, 1.25 MiB = 510, 1.5 MiB = 526, libsigrok's own 3,129,344 B = 396: all four aborted by the transport's own watchdog. A step at a power of two, both sides page multiples, queue budget fixed, is a per-allocation threshold in Chromium's path (the fresh device-service buffer, the shared-memory BigBuffer copy, the renderer's DOMArrayBuffer copy - 8.25), i.e. exactly what a reused libusb transfer never pays and why libsigrok reaches 800 MB/s with the same reads. `deriveStreamTuning` now keeps libsigrok's geometry below a 500 MB/s line rate and uses 768 KiB x 16 above it, and a new coalesceBytes delivers 8 MiB blocks to the sink because the interleaved store costs ~1.2 ms per append whatever its size (768 KiB -> 0.775-1.452 ms, 3.13 MB -> 2.185 ms, 8 MiB -> 5.025 ms) - per-read delivery would ask it for 1.5 s of work per second of data. End to end through the shipping app on the same board, 32ch/200M now receives 134,217,728 B (16 blocks) before the watchdog aborts at 648-654 MB/s, against 14 MB at 104 MB/s before the change; stubbing the frame loop's draw() moves it 510 -> 654 MB/s, so ~145 MB/s of the page's budget is the live renderer and the rest is the store (sink p95 7.2 ms per 8 MiB append, peakQueued 63 of 64). The pipe is no longer the limit - the page is - and that is the next piece of work, app-side. 155 offline checks green (4 new: the geometry gate, the coalescing block sizes, the byte stream through coalescing, the tail flush), tsc green. Still unmeasured: the real sampler at 32ch/200M (the raw upload's rate is not the sampler's), which needs the replug 8.24 has been waiting for - the watcher is still armed and will run the sweep on its own.

The queue was bounded by the consumer, and that is what wedged the board (fix in progress, NOTES 8.27). Device 002:112 through the shipping app: 32ch/100M got 12,517,372 B then aborted at 374 MB/s of the 400 the device offers, with peakQueued 17 of the 20-chunk lag cap the loop stops refilling at - the device was left with an empty queue and its FIFO overran, which is what libsigrok's own resubmit rule (bounded by samples_need_nbytes, never by the consumer, protocol.c:395) exists to prevent.
